text: There are n rooms, numbered from zero. Meetings are given as start and end times. Each meeting takes the free room with the lowest number. If no room is free, it waits for the first room to free up and keeps its length. When a room frees up, the meeting that originally started earlier goes first. Return the room that held the most meetings, the lowest number on a tie.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a meeting runs up to but not including its end time, so another meeting can start right at that moment? And are all start times different?
Yes to both. The end isn't included, and every start time is unique.

Okay. One thing I want to say early: picking a room follows two different rules. If some rooms are free, I want the lowest number. If none are free, I want the room that frees up first. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to a hundred rooms, up to ten to the fifth meetings, and times up to five hundred thousand.

Got it. One thing to note right away: delays stack up. A hundred thousand meetings, each up to half a million long, can push end times far past the int limit, so I'll use long long for times. Let me check example one: two rooms, zero to ten, one to five, two to seven, three to four. Rooms zero and one each end up with two meetings, so it's a tie, and the answer is zero.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would scan all n rooms for every meeting, which works since n is at most a hundred, but it depends on n being small. This problem reminds me of an event simulation with priority queues. Since there are two selection rules, I use two min-heaps: one of free room numbers, and one of busy rooms keyed by end time, then room number.
Why not a single heap of every room's available time?

Because once several rooms are already free, the rule cares about the room number, not which one freed up first. With two rooms and meetings zero to three, one to two, three to four: at time three both rooms are free, a single heap picks room one, but the answer needs room zero. Both official examples still pass with that version, so it's an easy bug to miss.

Here's the plan, in three steps. Sort by start. Before each meeting, move every busy room that ends at or before its start back to the free heap. Then, if a room is free, take the lowest number; otherwise take the busy room that frees first and delay the meeting to start there. One thing worth flagging — rule three, earlier meetings first, comes for free, because I process meetings in start order.

Alright. Two priority queues and a count per room. In the delay case, I pop the earliest busy room, set the new end to its end plus the meeting's length, and put the room back into the free heap, so both cases share the same assignment code. At the end I return the position of the max count, not the count itself. The easy lines to get wrong are the three I actually got wrong at first: returning the count, using a max-heap for free rooms, and storing the end in an int. The last one only fails on large inputs.

Let's dry-run example two: three rooms, expected one. The first three meetings each get a free room. The moment that matters is six to eight: no room is free, and rooms one and two both free up at ten. The pair comparison breaks the tie by number, so it goes to room one, ending at twelve. Counts are one, two, two, and the tie goes to room one. Corner cases: a single meeting uses room zero. One room with every meeting delayed still works with long long. Back-to-back meetings reuse room zero.

Let me think about complexity here. With m meetings and n rooms, sorting is m log m, and each meeting does a constant number of heap operations, each log n. So time is m log m plus m log n. Space is linear in n for the two heaps and the counts.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw that the two selection rules need two heaps, and showed why one heap fails. You caught the overflow from stacking delays before writing code. And you explained why the earlier-start rule needs no extra queue. Good work.
